Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Lesotho Mounted Police Service (LMPS) uses paper-based records like Occurrence Books (OB) for disciplinary cases, complaints registers, custody logs, and dockets at stations, including rural ones lacking electricity/telephones.APCOF Report Evidence of digital efforts: Integrated Case Management System (ICMS) login portal (v0.1.1), LMPS_RIMS project (2019+), GoLehokela digital policing platform. Courts use Synergy CMS integrating police data, but operational at limited urban sites (Maseru). No rural-specific digital rollout; rural stations rely on paper with later district entry possible. Predominantly paper with some digital pilots/urban systems = score 2.

revised_comments: Rural police stations in Lesotho continue to rely predominantly on paper-based recording, including Occurrence Books, custody logs and dockets, particularly where electricity and telecommunications are absent. Digitalisation efforts are underway but remain partial: the Lehokela community-policing application, developed with UNDP, the National University of Lesotho and Econet Telecom Lesotho, was officially launched nationally in April 2026 following a multi-year pilot, with phased rollout to police stations beginning in June 2026 and desktop computers being distributed to selected stations. Separately, the Ministry of Public Works and Transport began training police in Thaba-Tseka district in February 2026 to record road accidents digitally via the Road Accident Management System, replacing the manual LMPS 29 form. These initiatives indicate a transition in progress rather than a completed shift, with most rural stations still operating largely on paper alongside emerging digital tools.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Lesotho record administrative data, enrollment, attendance, and other metrics using paper-based Annual Statistical Census (ASC) forms filled by principals and submitted via district officers to the central Education Planning Unit.2023 Education Statistics Report This process remains manual at the point of service, with data later captured into central OpenEMIS for aggregated annual reporting, not real-time individual tracking.KIX EMIS Peer Review A 2017-2018 OpenEMIS pilot aimed at learner unit records was scaled back due to resource constraints, including lack of district statisticians, equipment, and internet.World Bank ICT Survey Only ~10/1477 primary schools have rudimentary ICT access (~20/1700 have electricity), severely limiting rural facilities (70% of population).KIX EMIS Peer Review Plans to shift to DHIS2 for Education emphasize district-level roles but no evidence of school-level digital rollout by 2023-2026. Key barriers: poor rural infrastructure, no electricity/internet, unqualified teachers (51% in mountains), funding gaps. National EMIS exists, but rural reality is entirely paper-based recording with central digitization—gap reflects ambition vs resource reality. (198 words)

revision_notes: All three original sources (2023 Education Statistics Report, KIX EMIS Peer Review, World Bank ICT Survey) were consistent with a paper-based facility-level recording process and support code 1. Fresh searches found a May 2026 DHIS2/HISP account of the new LEMIS system, which explicitly confirms that as of the 2025-2026 transition, schools still 'complete paper-based forms' and submit them to district offices; the LEMIS build is at ministry/district level (staff trained March 2026), not yet a school-level digital rollout. Per the variable's guidance to assess facility-level capture only, code 1 (Entirely paper) is confirmed with stronger, more current evidence than originally cited.
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Lesotho record enrolment, attendance and administrative data using paper-based Annual School Census forms, which are submitted to district offices for manual verification and data entry, a process that can take months. The Ministry of Education and Training, with UNICEF and HISP support, began developing a new national education management information system (LEMIS) on the DHIS2 platform in September 2025, covering 4,819 institutions, with core Ministry staff trained on the system in March 2026. As of mid-2026 this transition remains at the ministry and district level; data capture at the school level, including in rural facilities, is still entirely paper-based, consistent with limited ICT access and electricity in the great majority of rural primary schools.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: In rural primary healthcare clinics (health centers), patient data recording is predominantly paper-based for general care. Non-HIV/TB patients use paper health booklets, with data manually aggregated into national DHIS2 at higher levels MCC Blog 2023. For HIV/TB/PMTCT/cervical screening/pharmacy, eRegister EMR is deployed nationwide at all 170 government health centers (many rural) using decentralized local servers to handle poor connectivity/power; data auto-syncs to DHIS2 Oxford Digital Health 2024. Some duplicate paper processes persist. Digital systems are donor-driven (PEPFAR/ICAP) for specific diseases, not standard point-of-care for majority routine care. Pilots like village health worker tablets (BKM) exist but community-level. Barriers: unreliable power (outages, failing solar), low connectivity, technical capacity reliant on partners. MCC compact (2024+) plans expansion to all diseases, but currently not predominant at most rural clinics for all recording. Gap: National ambitions (Digital Health Strategy 2025-30 validated 2024) and HIV digital success contrast with paper-dominant routine rural PoC.

revision_notes: Original sources (MCC blog, PMC article, DHIS2 community post) describe the same picture: eRegister deployed across ~170-178 facilities for specific programmes (HIV, TB, ANC, cervical screening) while routine general care remains paper-based, supporting code 2. Fresh searches surfaced two 2025 peer-reviewed studies: a May 2025 cross-sectional study of eRegister use in Mafeteng district (17 facilities) confirming generally positive uptake but persistent electricity/connectivity barriers, and a November 2025 qualitative study confirming the eRegister covers five specific programmes and that government intends to phase out paper recording only once eRegister is fully operational nationwide - i.e. not yet the case. Code 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) is confirmed with more current sourcing.
revised_comments: Routine patient data recording in Lesotho's rural primary healthcare clinics remains predominantly paper-based, with paper health booklets used for most general care and data manually aggregated into DHIS2 at higher levels. For HIV, TB, antenatal and cervical-screening services, an electronic register (eRegister, built on the Bahmni platform) is deployed across more than 170 government health facilities nationwide, including many rural sites, using decentralised local servers to cope with unreliable power and connectivity, with data automatically synchronised to DHIS2. Studies from 2025 describe generally positive healthcare-worker perceptions of the eRegister but confirm that network connectivity and electricity outages remain significant operational barriers, and that the government envisages paper-based recording being phased out only once the eRegister is fully operational nationwide. Routine point-of-care recording for the majority of rural clinic services therefore remains paper-based alongside disease-specific digital systems.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices and civil registration points in Lesotho predominantly use paper-based forms for birth registration, with records later digitized and transferred electronically to regional/national databases. UNECA APAI-CRVS Report (2023) confirms electronic transfer from local offices but Lesotho not among countries with universal district-level electronic entry. Automated digital systems for point-of-service electronic recording and immediate certification piloted in ~4 hospitals (since 2021) and select rural community councils (e.g., Qanya CC in Qacha’s Nek, 2022), supported by UNICEF. Lesotho Ministry of Home Affairs; Gov Lesotho. National CRVS Strategic Plan (2020-2024) promotes decentralization to chiefs/councils and digitalisation, with 2023 Ntlafatsa Bana system and 2024-2026 DPI commitments, but 2025 UNICEF consultancy reviews incomplete scale-up. Barriers: Rural infrastructure gaps (electricity/connectivity in 70% mountainous terrain), low digital literacy, staffing shortages. Gap: National electronic aggregation ambition vs. paper-default at most ~10,000 rural points; pilots cover minority of facilities, fitting score 2.

revision_notes: Original sources (APAI-CRVS report, Home Affairs Qanya community council article, gov.ls automated birth registration launch) were consistent with a picture of paper-default rural registration alongside a growing set of digital pilots, supporting code 2. Fresh searches found a June 2025 UN Lesotho account of the Ntlafatsa Bana programme's real-time tablet-based birth registration (integrated with the NISSA social registry) expanding to further community councils, a January 2026 outreach report from Qacha's Nek confirming hard-to-reach villages still rely on manual, in-person registration events and that transport shortages constrain decentralisation, and a February 2026 government announcement of a new MOSIP-based digital identity work plan with UNICEF running through 2026-2028. Together these confirm code 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) remains correct, with digitalisation still a minority-coverage, in-progress effort rather than the rural default.
revised_comments: Civil registration in Lesotho's rural areas is predominantly paper-based, delivered through outreach by Civil Registration Officers and, since 2020, through deployment at health facilities and community councils. Digital birth registration has expanded through the EU/UNICEF-supported Ntlafatsa Bana programme, which uses real-time tablet-based registration operated by Village Health Workers and Civil Registration Officers, integrated with the NISSA social assistance database, in selected community councils such as Qhoasing. However, coverage of automated registration remains limited to a minority of community councils and health facilities; a January 2026 outreach in Qacha's Nek highlights that hard-to-reach mountain villages still rely on manual, in-person registration events, and officials note that decentralisation to councils is constrained by transport and logistics. The Ministry of Information, Communications, Science, Technology and Innovation and UNICEF signed a 2026 work plan to continue developing a MOSIP-based digital identity ecosystem linked to civil registration, indicating that national-level digitalisation remains a work in progress rather than complete.
